about.title: About Terra Tempora
about.why1: History books usually show one map at a time: the Roman Empire at its height, Europe in 1815, the Mongol conquests. Each map is clear on its own, but it is hard to see what came before, what came after, and who else lived on the planet at the same moment.
about.why2: Terra Tempora was made to fill that gap. It puts the borders of more than 1,500 civilizations on a single globe and lets you move freely through time, from the first states to today. You can watch realms rise, spread, meet and fall, and see how the world we live in took shape.
about.why3: It is an amateur project, made out of curiosity and a love of history, for anyone who wants to understand the past a little better: students, teachers, travellers or simply curious minds.
about.data: The borders come from Cliopatria, the open dataset of the Seshat Global History Databank. Key figures, links between realms and events come from Wikidata and Wikipedia, and pictures from Wikimedia Commons. All of this is the work of researchers and volunteers who share it freely; the Sources button lists them in full.
about.care: In the past, borders were rarely sharp lines: many realms had shifting frontiers, vassals, or lands they claimed but barely controlled. The shapes shown here are approximations, and some dates and names are still debated by historians. If you spot a mistake or something missing, please tell us: every report is read.
about.privacy: Terra Tempora has no account, no advertising and no cookies. It counts visits anonymously, with no IP address and nothing that identifies you, to learn which parts of the site are used. The privacy and legal notice says what is collected and why, and how to reach us at privacy@terra-tempora.com.
about.credit: This project was built with AI, carefully prompted with ❤️ using Claude Opus 5.5.

panel.intro: This is an amateur website to learn about the history of civilizations, mapped directly onto the Earth. Use the timeline at the bottom to travel through time, also four modes are available from the burger menu at the top left and below:

modes.travel: Fly through almost 12,000 years of history, from Göbekli Tepe to COVID-19, with the pyramids, great wars, treaties and discoveries mapped on the planet along the way.
modes.civilizations: Watch civilizations rise, expand and fall on the map, with the related realms around them, to understand how they interacted.
modes.countries: Ever wondered which civilizations lived within the borders of a modern country long ago? This mode shows you every nation that once crossed the borders of a given country.
modes.nations: In this mode, discover every civilization that led to a nation of today, from its earliest roots to the present, even those that stood far from its current borders.

sources.list:
• Borders: Cliopatria, Seshat Global History Databank, CC BY 4.0: the realms of 3400 BCE to 2024, simplified for display. Today’s countries are its realms of 2024, drawn until the current year.
  • Borders of Magadha and its successors (the Nanda, Maurya and Shunga empires, 600 to 171 BCE): traced from Magadha Expansion by Avantiputra7, after Schwartzberg’s Historical Atlas of South Asia, CC BY-SA 4.0; the traced borders are shared under the same licence.
  • Borders of the Bamana Empire of Ségou (1766 to 1802), Kaarta, Kong and the Mossi and Hausa kingdoms: traced from Africa de l’Oèst (fin sègle XVIII) by Nicolas Eynaud, CC BY-SA 4.0; the traced borders are shared under the same licence.
  • Borders of the Luba Empire: traced from Lunda Empire, Library of Congress (Zaire: A Country Study, 1994, after Jan Vansina’s Kingdoms of the Savanna), public domain.
  • Borders of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe: taken from African civilizations map (pre-colonial) by Jeff Israel, CC BY-SA 3.0; the borders are shared under the same licence.
  • Civilization names in other languages, key figures and links between realms: Wikidata, CC0.
  • Card pictures: the realm’s picture, coat of arms or flag on Wikidata, or else the lead picture of its English Wikipedia article; every file is on Wikimedia Commons and is credited with its author and licence.
  • Realm overviews: the opening paragraph of the realm’s Wikipedia article, in the reader’s language when there is one (CC BY-SA 4.0), with the photos and videos the article shows, kept only when they are on Wikimedia Commons, each credited with its author and licence.
  • Events: the Mongol ones written for this site from standard references; the others from Wikidata (CC0), with the opening paragraph of their Wikipedia article (CC BY-SA 4.0); pictures from the events’ Wikipedia articles, shown only when the file is on Wikimedia Commons, with its author and licence.
  • History travel: the turning points were chosen and written for this site from standard references; each links to its Wikipedia article and to searches on Britannica and World History Encyclopedia.
  • Documentaries: hand-picked, each linked to its page on Netflix, National Geographic, Discovery Channel or History Channel.
  • Globe imagery: Natural Earth II, public domain, as packaged with CesiumJS (Apache 2.0).
  • Map coastlines: Natural Earth 1:50m land, public domain, via world-atlas (ISC), read with topojson-client (ISC). Projections by d3-geo and d3-geo-projection (ISC).
  • Fonts: Newsreader (Production Type) and Instrument Sans (Instrument), SIL Open Font License 1.1, served with the site through Fontsource.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Workers, which also keeps the anonymous usage counts and checks reports for spam (Turnstile). The privacy and legal notice has the details.
